chapter_summary:
Once you have built a Docker image, the next crucial step is to manage the containers created from that image. A Docker container has a well-defined lifecycle: it's created, started, potentially paused, stopped, and eventually removed. Understanding this lifecycle and the commands to control it is fundamental to operating Docker effectively in any environment. Just as you manage processes on a traditional server, you'll manage containers, but with the added benefits of isolation and portability that Docker provides.

Let's dive into the core commands for container management. The most basic command to see what containers are currently running is `docker ps`. This command lists all *running* containers, showing their Container ID, Image, Command, Creation time, Status, Ports, and Name. If you want to see all containers, including those that have exited, you use `docker ps -a`. This is incredibly useful for debugging or cleaning up old containers. For example, after running our `hello-world` container, `docker ps` would show nothing, but `docker ps -a` would list it with an "Exited" status.

To start a container from an image, you use `docker run`. We saw this with `docker run hello-world`. When you run `docker run my-flask-app:1.0`, Docker creates a new container instance from the `my-flask-app:1.0` image and starts it. By default, `docker run` runs the container in the foreground, meaning its output is streamed to your terminal, and your terminal is blocked until the container exits. For long-running applications like web servers, this isn't practical. Instead, you'll want to run containers in **detached mode** using the `-d` flag: `docker run -d -p 8000:5000 my-flask-app:1.0`. This starts the container in the background and prints its Container ID to your terminal, allowing you to continue using your terminal for other tasks.

Once a container is running in detached mode, you might need to view its output or logs. The `docker logs` command is your go-to for this. For example, `docker logs <container_id_or_name>` will display the standard output and standard error streams of your container. You can also follow the logs in real-time with `docker logs -f <container_id_or_name>`, similar to `tail -f` on Linux.

To stop a running container, you use `docker stop <container_id_or_name>`. This sends a `SIGTERM` signal to the main process inside the container, giving it a grace period (default 10 seconds) to shut down cleanly. If the container doesn't stop within this period, Docker sends a `SIGKILL` to force termination. If you need to immediately stop a container without a grace period, you can use `docker kill <container_id_or_name>`. After stopping, a container still exists but is not running. To restart a stopped container, use `docker start <container_id_or_name>`. If you want to stop and then start a container, `docker restart <container_id_or_name>` combines these actions.

When a container is no longer needed, it's good practice to remove it to free up resources. `docker rm <container_id_or_name>` removes a stopped container. If you try to remove a running container, Docker will complain. You can force removal of a running container with `docker rm -f <container_id_or_name>`, but it's generally better to stop it first. To remove all stopped containers, a useful command is `docker container prune`. This helps keep your system clean.

Sometimes, you need to run a command inside an already running container for debugging or administrative tasks. This is where `docker exec` comes in handy. For instance, to open a bash shell inside your running Flask application container, you would use `docker exec -it <container_id_or_name> bash`. The `-i` flag keeps `STDIN` open even if not attached, and `-t` allocates a pseudo-TTY, which makes the shell interactive. This allows you to explore the container's filesystem, check processes, or run diagnostics directly within its isolated environment.

A critical aspect of running web applications in containers is making them accessible from the outside world. This is achieved through **port mapping**. When you run `docker run -p 8000:5000 my-flask-app:1.0`, you are mapping port `8000` on your host machine to port `5000` inside the container. This means any traffic coming into your host on port 8000 will be forwarded to port 5000 of the container. Without port mapping, your application inside the container, even if it's listening on port 5000, would not be reachable from outside the container's isolated network. You can map multiple ports or let Docker assign a random host port with `-p 5000`.

**Inspecting containers** is another powerful debugging tool. `docker inspect <container_id_or_name>` provides a wealth of detailed information about a container in JSON format, including its network settings, volumes, environment variables, and more. This is invaluable when trying to understand how a container is configured or why it might not be behaving as expected.

**Common mistakes and safety notes:**
*   **Forgetting to stop/remove containers:** This can lead to resource exhaustion (disk space, memory) over time, especially with many exited containers or logs. Regularly prune stopped containers and unused images (`docker image prune`).
*   **Port conflicts:** Trying to map a container port to a host port that is already in use by another process (Docker container or otherwise) will result in an error. Use `docker ps` to check occupied ports or choose a different host port.
*   **Not running in detached mode:** Running long-lived applications without `-d` will block your terminal, which is inconvenient.
*   **Using `docker kill` instead of `docker stop`:** While `kill` is faster, `stop` allows the application to shut down gracefully, preventing data corruption or incomplete operations. Only use `kill` when a graceful shutdown fails.
*   **Security:** Be cautious when using `docker exec` to run commands inside containers, especially if the container is running with elevated privileges. Avoid installing unnecessary tools or keeping sensitive data inside containers.

Mastering these container management commands forms the backbone of deploying and maintaining containerized applications, a core skill for any professional working with IBM DevOps and cloud-native technologies.

screens.title: Managing Docker Containers
screens.subtitle: From lifecycle to everyday commands — list, run, inspect, and clean containers safely

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn to operate containers confidently. Containers follow a lifecycle: they are created from images, started, may be paused, stopped, and finally removed. Managing that lifecycle with Docker CLI commands is a core operational skill. You will see how to observe running containers, start an image in the foreground or background, read logs, run commands inside a container for debugging, map host ports to make services reachable, and reliably remove containers when they are no longer needed. The practical examples use a Flask application image and the familiar commands you will use daily, such as docker ps, docker run -d with -p for port mapping, docker logs -f for live output, docker exec -it for an interactive shell, and docker rm or docker container prune to reclaim space. You will also learn common mistakes to watch for, like port conflicts or leaving many exited containers behind. By the end, you will be able to start, inspect, debug, and clean containers in a way that keeps your workspace tidy and your services reachable. Think about a time you had a blocked terminal or an unreachable web app — this chapter shows the exact commands to avoid those pitfalls.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Container management is about lifecycle control, observability, and safe cleanup — using a small set of Docker CLI commands to run, debug, and remove containers while avoiding resource and port conflicts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Managing Docker Containers
Managing Docker Containers
Control lifecycle, read logs, run commands inside containers, and expose services safely.

This lesson focuses on the practical CLI operations you will use every day. Expect concrete commands, examples using a Flask app image, and safety tips to avoid common mistakes like port conflicts and abandoned containers.

You will practice starting containers detached, following logs in real time, entering a running container to inspect files, and cleaning up stopped containers to reclaim resources.

In this lesson

Create, run, stop, remove — the sequence and the commands you need.
Inspect & debug

Explore Key Topics

States from creation to removal and why each matters for cleanup.
Command Set
docker ps, run, logs, exec, stop, rm and inspect — the daily toolkit.
Troubleshooting
Port conflicts, orphaned containers, and graceful shutdowns to avoid data loss.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will manage containers across their full lifecycle. First, you will name and list containers, distinguishing running versus exited instances. Second, you will run images in foreground and detached modes, and map host ports so services are reachable from your machine. Third, you will inspect and debug containers: stream logs in real time and run an interactive shell inside a running container to check files or processes. Fourth, you will remove stopped containers and prune unused ones to avoid resource exhaustion, and you will recognize common mistakes like port conflicts or using forceful termination when a graceful stop is appropriate. Each objective links a practical command to a concrete operation: docker ps and docker ps -a to observe state; docker run -d -p to start detached with port mapping; docker logs -f and docker exec -it to debug; docker rm and docker container prune to clean up. Practicing these steps with a simple Flask image gives you repeatable workflows you can reuse with other services. You will also learn the safety mindset: prefer graceful shutdowns and stop before removing, and check ports before mapping a host port. This makes container operations predictable and safe in development and production.

keyIdea.text: Manage, observe, debug, and clean containers using a focused set of Docker CLI commands and safe operational practices.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Why They Matter
screens.subtitle: Practical skills tied to commands and safe habits

narration.text: These objectives are expressed as practical skills so you can apply them immediately. You will learn to interpret docker ps output: Container ID, image, command, status, ports, and name — this helps you quickly find a running service or identify an exited process that needs cleanup. You will practice starting images with docker run and understand the difference between foreground runs, which stream output to your terminal, and detached runs with -d, which let the terminal remain free. You will also practice docker logs to read standard output and standard error, including following logs in real time with docker logs -f. For deeper inspection, docker inspect returns JSON metadata that shows ports, networks, volumes, and environment variables — useful when behavior depends on configuration. Finally, you will learn to use docker exec -it to open a shell inside a running container for troubleshooting, then stop and remove containers responsibly. Each skill prevents a real operational pain: blocked terminals, invisible services, or wasted disk space. Build these skills now and you will save time and reduce surprises during development and deployment.

keyIdea.text: Combine command knowledge with a safety-first workflow: observe, run detached, debug, and clean — repeatably.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Learning Objectives
Objective details
  • Interpret output: Recognize running vs exited containers, and read port mappings like 0.0.0.0:8000->5000/tcp to verify access.
  • Run modes: Foreground runs block your terminal; detached runs use -d so services run in the background with a printed container ID.
  • Debugging: Use docker logs -f to stream logs and docker exec -it to open a shell for interactive checks.
  • Cleaning: Remove stopped containers with docker rm and reclaim resources with docker container prune when appropriate.
Micro-mnemonics
PS = present state; PS -A = all states
RUN in foreground = stream output; RUN -D = free terminal
LOGS = read output; EXEC = go inside

narration.text: A container's lifecycle is the sequence of states it moves through from creation to deletion. When you run docker run, Docker creates a new container instance from an image and attempts to start its main process. If the process is running, the container is in the running state. You might pause a container temporarily, for example to free C P U, but more commonly you stop a container when the main process exits or you request a graceful shutdown with docker stop. A stopped container still exists on disk with its filesystem and metadata intact; it just isn't running. Removing a container with docker rm deletes that instance's metadata and writable layer so you cannot restart it. Understanding these states helps you reason about commands: docker ps shows running containers only, while docker ps -a shows all states including exited. A common misconception is that stopping a container deletes it — it does not. Another is that images are containers — images are templates, containers are runtime instances. Example: after running docker run hello-world, the program exits immediately; docker ps will not list it, but docker ps -a will show an Exited entry. Key takeaway: map the command you need to the lifecycle state you intend to reach, and prefer stop before rm to avoid accidental data loss. How will you check whether a container you stopped still exists?

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle clarity
keyIdea.text: Containers are runtime instances of images and pass through distinct states; commands act on specific states so choose them intentionally.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Container lifecycle
Definition
A container is a runtime instance of an image. It has a state: created, running, paused, stopped (exited), and removed. Commands change or observe those states.
Created: docker creates the instance but not necessarily started.
Running: main process is active and serving requests if applicable.
Stopped/Exited: process ended; container remains until removed.
Removed: container instance and writable layer are deleted.
Key Takeaway

Use docker ps to check running state and docker ps -a to discover stopped instances before removing.

Concrete example
Run a short-lived container to verify behavior:
$ docker run hello-world
# The image runs, prints a message, then exits.
After that, docker ps returns nothing, while docker ps -a lists the exited container. This distinction helps you locate containers that need removal or inspection.
Misconception: stopping a container deletes it. It does not; it remains until you remove it.
Pro tip: prefer docker stop so the app can shut down cleanly and flush state.

screens.title: Listing containers with docker ps
screens.subtitle: Find running and stopped containers and read their key fields

narration.text: docker ps is the first command you use to understand what is currently running. By default it lists only running containers and shows helpful columns such as Container ID, Image, Command, Creation time, Status, Ports, and Name. If you don't see your container there, it might have exited; in that case docker ps -a lists all containers including those that have stopped. Learning to read the ports column is essential for verifying accessibility — it shows host-to-container mappings like 0.0.0.0:8000->5000/tcp. Common use patterns include piping docker ps output to additional tools to filter or using the --format flag for concise reporting, but the basic command is often all you need. A common beginner mistake is assuming docker ps always shows everything; remember the -a flag. Concrete example: after starting the Flask app in detached mode with docker run -d -p 8000:5000 --name my-flask-web-app my-flask-app:1.0, run docker ps to confirm you see my-flask-web-app listed and the port mapping. If the port mapping is missing, the service may not have been started with -p, meaning it won't be reachable from your host. Closing question: when you see an Exited status, what next step will you take to diagnose why it stopped?

keyIdea.title: Observation
keyIdea.text: Use docker ps and docker ps -a to find containers and verify port mappings and runtime status before acting.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › docker ps
Command & output
$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE                 COMMAND                  CREATED       STATUS       PORTS                    NAMES
4f3b2c9c1e2a   my-flask-app:1.0      "python app.py"         2 minutes ago Up 2 minutes 0.0.0.0:8000->5000/tcp  my-flask-web-app
Notice the Ports column: host port 8000 is forwarded to container port 5000. If a container is not listed, run docker ps -a to see exited entries.
Quick checklist
  • Use docker ps to find running containers.
  • Use docker ps -a to include exited containers for debugging.
  • Confirm port mappings show host:container relationships.
  • If missing, re-run with -p host:container to expose the service.
Misconception: docker ps shows every container. It only shows running ones unless you add -a.

screens.title: Running a container and detached mode
screens.subtitle: docker run, foreground vs detached (-d), naming, and port mapping

narration.text: docker run is how you create a container and start it in a single command. A beginner pitfall is not understanding run's default behavior: without -d it runs in the foreground and binds your terminal to the container's output. For long-lived services like a web server, use -d to run detached so Docker prints a container ID and returns control to your terminal. Use --name to give a friendly identifier rather than relying on the auto-generated name. To make your service reachable, map a host port to a container port using -p host:container. For example: docker run -d -p 8000:5000 --name my-flask-web-app my-flask-app:1.0 starts the Flask server in the background and maps host port 8000 to the app's listening port 5000. A frequent mistake is forgetting -p; the app runs, but it is unreachable from the host. Another is failing to use --name and then repeatedly searching for the container ID. Practice: start the container with -d and confirm docker ps shows it. If the terminal was blocked earlier when you ran without -d, stop that run with Ctrl+C and restart properly. Key takeaway: choose -d for services and -p to publish ports so your application can serve traffic.

keyIdea.title: Start with intent
keyIdea.text: Decide if a container should run interactively or detached, and always map ports when you need external access.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › docker run
Run examples
$ docker run my-flask-app:1.0
# Runs in foreground; terminal is attached to container output.

$ docker run -d -p 8000:5000 --name my-flask-web-app my-flask-app:1.0
# Runs in background and maps host port 8000 to container 5000.
Use --name to simplify later commands like docker logs my-flask-web-app or docker exec -it my-flask-web-app bash.
Common mistakes & checks
  • Forgetting -d: your terminal will be blocked until the container exits.
  • Forgetting -p: service may be running but not reachable from host.
  • Not naming containers: harder to reference by ID later.
Try it: start detached, run docker ps, and then docker logs to ensure the server started successfully.

screens.title: Viewing container output with docker logs
screens.subtitle: Read past output and follow logs in real time

narration.text: docker logs shows the stdout and stderr streams produced by a container's main process. Use docker logs to print accumulated logs. To watch logs as they arrive, add -f to follow them similar to tail -f. This is invaluable when running containers in detached mode because you can still observe runtime behavior without attaching your terminal to the process. Example: after starting my-flask-web-app with docker run -d -p 8000:5000 --name my-flask-web-app my-flask-app:1.0, docker logs my-flask-web-app prints the server startup messages; docker logs -f my-flask-web-app streams new requests or error traces live. A misconception is thinking logs replace structured monitoring; they are a simple and immediate way to investigate startup failures and runtime exceptions. If logs show the server did not bind to the expected port, check your application configuration and the docker run -p mapping. Key takeaway: use logs to confirm the service started, diagnose errors, and then use docker exec for deeper inspection when logs aren't sufficient. How would you use logs and exec together to find a missing dependency inside a container? Viewing container output with docker logs means docker logs and docker logs -f provide quick visibility into what a container is doing, especially when run detached.. In practical terms, read past output and follow logs in real time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Observability
keyIdea.text: docker logs and docker logs -f provide quick visibility into what a container is doing, especially when run detached.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › docker logs
Commands
$ docker logs my-flask-web-app
# show recent output

$ docker logs -f my-flask-web-app
# follow logs in real time (Ctrl+C to stop following)
Following logs is helpful when you trigger requests from a browser or an API client and want to observe resulting output live.
When to use exec
If logs indicate missing files or failing processes, run docker exec -it bash to peek into the filesystem and run diagnostics. Logs and exec together provide fast root-cause analysis.
Misconception: logs always contain full context. Some runtime issues require interactive inspection inside the container.

screens.title: Stopping and restarting containers
screens.subtitle: docker stop, docker kill, docker start, and docker restart

narration.text: Stopping a container is part of normal operations. docker stop sends a SIGTERM to the container's main process and waits a grace period (typically ten seconds) for a clean shutdown. If the process doesn't exit, Docker escalates to SIGKILL to force termination. Use docker kill only when you need immediate termination — killing does not allow graceful cleanup and can cause incomplete writes. After stopping, the container still exists and can be restarted with docker start. To stop and immediately start, docker restart performs both actions for you. Practical example: if a Flask server is not responding, try docker stop my-flask-web-app, then docker start my-flask-web-app to restart it; use docker restart my-flask-web-app as a shorthand. A common mistake is habitually using docker kill; prefer stop so applications have the chance to flush buffers and close files. If a container ignores stop consistently, consider investigating its shutdown handlers or using kill as a last resort. Key takeaway: prefer graceful stop, and use restart when you need a quick cycle that preserves container identity and configuration. Stopping and restarting containers means prefer docker stop to give processes time to exit cleanly; use kill only when stop fails and investigate the cause.. In practical terms, docker stop, docker kill, docker start, and docker restart. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Graceful shutdown
keyIdea.text: Prefer docker stop to give processes time to exit cleanly; use kill only when stop fails and investigate the cause.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › stop / restart
Commands & behavior
$ docker stop my-flask-web-app
# sends SIGTERM, waits for graceful shutdown

$ docker kill my-flask-web-app
# sends SIGKILL immediately

$ docker start my-flask-web-app
# starts an existing stopped container

$ docker restart my-flask-web-app
# stop then start in one command
Checks and tips
  • If stop doesn't work, check logs for shutdown errors before using kill.
  • Restart preserves the container's identity and any attached volumes; it does not recreate an instance from the image.
  • To permanently get rid of an instance use docker rm after stopping.
Mistake to avoid: using kill as the default stop mechanism. Save kill for stuck processes only.

screens.title: Removing containers and pruning
screens.subtitle: docker rm, docker rm -f, docker container prune

narration.text: When a container is no longer needed, remove it to free disk and metadata. docker rm deletes a stopped container; if you attempt to remove a running container, Docker will prevent it. You can force removal with docker rm -f, but this is equivalent to sending SIGKILL and then removing the instance, which may leave incomplete state. To clean up many stopped containers at once, docker container prune removes all stopped containers and helps reclaim space. Regular pruning is good hygiene, especially during iterative development where many short-lived containers accumulate. A common oversight is leaving exited containers on the host; over time logs and writable layers consume disk. Example: after stopping my-flask-web-app with docker stop my-flask-web-app, run docker rm my-flask-web-app to remove it. If you prefer bulk cleanup after testing, docker container prune achieves the same in a single command. Key takeaway: stop before remove whenever possible, and use prune to reclaim resources responsibly. Removing containers and pruning means remove stopped containers to free resources; use container prune for bulk cleanup but avoid forcing removal of running containers.. In practical terms, docker rm, docker rm -f, docker container prune. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cleanup
keyIdea.text: Remove stopped containers to free resources; use container prune for bulk cleanup but avoid forcing removal of running containers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Remove & prune
Commands
$ docker stop my-flask-web-app
$ docker rm my-flask-web-app

# Force remove (not recommended unless necessary)
$ docker rm -f my-flask-web-app

# Remove all stopped containers
$ docker container prune
When to prune
Prune after a development session or CI run when you have many exited containers. Be cautious on shared hosts; pruning removes stopped containers globally.
Pro tip: run docker ps -a before pruning to review what will be removed, preventing accidental deletion of valuable stopped containers.

screens.title: Execute commands inside a running container
screens.subtitle: docker exec -it to run a shell and inspect a container

narration.text: docker exec lets you run a command inside a running container; the most common use is to open an interactive shell for troubleshooting. The flags -i and -t combine to keep STDIN open and allocate a pseudo-TTY, producing a usable shell session. Example: docker exec -it my-flask-web-app bash opens a bash shell inside the container, allowing you to list files, check logs, run tests, or inspect environment variables. This is essential when logs alone don't reveal the issue. A common misconception is that exec requires rebuilding the image; it does not — it operates on the running instance. Use exec carefully when containers run with elevated privileges or hold sensitive data. After you finish, type exit to leave the container shell. If a container does not have bash, try sh instead. Key takeaway: use exec for interactive debugging and to run one-off administrative commands inside a container without changing the image or restarting the service. Execute commands inside a running container means use docker exec -it to open a shell inside a running container for direct inspection and on-the-fly debugging.. In practical terms, docker exec -it to run a shell and inspect a container. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interactive inspection
keyIdea.text: Use docker exec -it to open a shell inside a running container for direct inspection and on-the-fly debugging.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › docker exec
Usage
$ docker exec -it my-flask-web-app bash
# interactive shell inside container

$ docker exec -it my-flask-web-app sh
# fallback if bash is not available

# inside the container
# ls -l /app
# exit
Safety & tips
Avoid making persistent changes inside containers used as ephemeral instances. Prefer rebuilding the image for long-term changes. Use exec for inspection and one-off fixes during development.
Misconception: exec requires restart. It does not: exec runs commands inside the running container without restarting it.

screens.title: Port mapping: make container services reachable
screens.subtitle: Understand -p host:container and host-to-container routing

narration.text: Port mapping links a port on your host machine to a port inside the container so services can be reached from outside the container's isolated network. When you run docker run -p 8000:5000 my-flask-app:1.0 you tell Docker to forward traffic arriving at host port 8000 to port 5000 inside the container, where the Flask app listens. Without this mapping, the application is running but not accessible from the host. You can map multiple ports or request a random host port by specifying only the container port. To verify mappings, run docker ps and inspect the Ports column where mappings appear as hostIP:hostPort->containerPort/tcp. A frequent problem is port conflict, where the chosen host port is already in use; Docker will return an error. To avoid conflicts, pick unused host ports or stop the process occupying the port, and use docker ps to check. Key takeaway: always decide the host port intentionally, verify docker ps shows the mapping, and test access in a browser using the host port. How will you check whether another process already occupies your desired host port before mapping it?

keyIdea.title: Expose services
keyIdea.text: Use -p host:container to forward traffic from the host into the container and verify via docker ps and browser requests.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Port mapping
Example
$ docker run -d -p 8000:5000 --name my-flask-web-app my-flask-app:1.0
# Host port 8000 forwards to container port 5000

# Then open http://localhost:8000 in your browser
If the browser can't reach the app, confirm the mapping with docker ps and check for port conflicts on the host.
Troubleshooting
  • Use docker ps to verify the Ports column shows the expected mapping.
  • If Docker errors on run, another process may be using the host port — choose a different host port or stop that process.
  • Remember internal container port must match the service's listening port.
Misconception: mapping a port exposes all container services. It only forwards traffic to the specified container port.

screens.title: Inspecting containers with docker inspect
screens.subtitle: Retrieve low-level configuration and network details

narration.text: docker inspect returns detailed JSON metadata about a container, image, network, or volume. For containers this output includes network settings, port bindings, mounted volumes, environment variables, entrypoint and command, and other runtime details. Use it when you need to know exactly how Docker configured the instance and why it might not be reachable. For example, docker inspect my-flask-web-app will reveal the container's IP, the HostConfig port bindings that map host ports to container ports, and environment entries passed at runtime. This is particularly helpful when automation or orchestration layers alter configuration and you need to verify the actual runtime parameters. A common misconception is that docker inspect is only for advanced users — in fact, it is the definitive source of truth for container configuration. Key takeaway: when behavior differs from expectation, inspect the container metadata to confirm networks, ports, and environment variables are set as intended. Inspecting containers with docker inspect means docker inspect returns the full runtime json for a container and is the primary tool for low-level debugging.. In practical terms, retrieve low-level configuration and network details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Example output snippet
$ docker inspect my-flask-web-app
[
  {
    "Id": "4f3b2c9c1e2a...",

    "NetworkSettings": {

Inspect the Ports and NetworkSettings sections to confirm mapping and container IP. Use this data when diagnosing access problems or verifying environment variables passed at runtime.
When to inspect
  • When docker ps shows a running container but the service is unreachable.
  • When automation populates environment variables and you want to verify they are present at runtime.
  • When port mappings appear different than expected.
Pro tip: pipe inspect to a JSON parser or use --format to extract specific fields for automation checks.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting checklist
screens.subtitle: Port conflicts, orphaned containers, and forceful termination dangers

narration.text: Container management often trips up learners with a few recurring mistakes. First, port conflicts: mapping to a host port already in use will cause docker run to fail. Check docker ps and your host processes before picking a port, or map to a different host port. Second, forgetting to stop and remove containers creates many exited instances that consume disk and log space; periodically run docker container prune after reviewing active containers. Third, overusing docker kill defeats graceful shutdown and can lead to data corruption for apps that require cleanup on SIGTERM. Fourth, running with elevated privileges and then exec-ing inside a container can expose sensitive data or allow accidental system changes. For each issue, there is a straightforward diagnostic: if docker run fails, read the error for port binding conflicts; if services are unreachable, verify docker ps Ports and docker inspect NetworkSettings; if behavior is unexpected, consult docker logs -f and then docker exec -it to inspect files. Example checklist: 1) docker ps -a to list containers, 2) docker logs -f to stream output, 3) docker inspect to verify configuration, 4) docker exec to run interactive checks. Key takeaway: a short checklist and conservative habits prevent most operational problems.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a short diagnostic sequence—ps, logs, inspect, exec—and prefer graceful stop and intentional cleanup to avoid common problems.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Troubleshooting checklist
Checklist
  1. docker ps -a — find running and stopped containers.
  2. docker logs -f <name> — observe output while exercising the app.
  3. docker inspect <name> — confirm ports and env settings.
  4. docker exec -it <name> bash — interactively inspect the filesystem.
Common issues
Port conflict: choose a different host port or stop the conflicting process.
Orphaned containers: remove stopped instances to free space.
Overuse of kill: prefer stop to allow graceful shutdowns.
Pro tip: include --name when running containers to make these commands easier and less error-prone.

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts you should retain. Containers follow a lifecycle: created, running, paused, stopped, and removed; choose commands that match the state you need. docker ps shows running containers; docker ps -a includes exited instances. Detached mode (-d) runs containers in the background while docker logs and docker logs -f let you inspect output. Use docker exec -it to open an interactive shell for investigation without rebuilding the image. Map host ports to container ports with -p host:container so services can be reached from your machine, and verify mappings with docker ps and docker inspect. Remove stopped containers with docker rm and use docker container prune for bulk cleanup. Prefer docker stop for graceful shutdowns and avoid overusing docker kill. These core practices make container management predictable and reduce resource and accessibility problems. Keep this checklist in mind as a routine: observe, debug, inspect, and clean. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three short reminders for daily practice

narration.text: Keep three short reminders handy as you work with containers. First, always confirm what is running with docker ps and include -a when you need to see exited containers. Second, decide how to run your service: for development experiments you may run in the foreground, but production-like services should run detached with -d and explicit port mapping using -p host:container. Third, debug with intent: use docker logs to read output, then docker exec -it to inspect the container environment if the logs don't reveal the issue. Clean up stopped containers regularly with docker rm and docker container prune so you avoid wasted disk space. These simple habits prevent most operational headaches and make container operations predictable. Which two reminders will you add to your daily checklist?
